sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish between over-the-counter and prescription medications, including how each category is regulated and labeled.
- Describe the medication reconciliation process, including collecting, comparing, verifying, and communicating a complete medication list.
- Explain why a complete medication list that includes OTC drugs and supplements is essential for preventing interactions, duplications, and omissions.
- Apply safe, within-scope practices for documenting OTC and supplement use and escalating discrepancies to licensed staff.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An OTC medicine is like a snack you can grab off the store shelf yourself, while a prescription is like food you can only get after a grown-up with a special badge writes a note for you.

### Question 2

Think of a prescription as a ticket you can only get after a doctor checks you and says 'yes, this is right for you.' An OTC medicine is one the store lets you buy after reading the box instructions.

### Question 3

The FDA is like the referee who decides which medicines are safe enough for people to buy on their own and which need a doctor's note first.

### Question 4

Just because you can buy something without a note doesn't mean you can't get hurt by using it the wrong way — like how you can still get a tummy ache from eating too much candy that was fine to buy.

### Question 5

A prescription medicine is like a special tool the doctor hands you after checking what's wrong; ibuprofen on the shelf and cough drops are things you can pick up yourself.

### Question 6

If a medicine needs a doctor to check you, pick the right amount, and watch how it's working, it stays 'prescription only' — like needing a coach for a tricky sport instead of playing in the yard on your own.

### Question 7

Acetaminophen for a headache is something you can buy yourself; antibiotics, insulin, and blood pressure pills all need a doctor's order.

### Question 8

The Drug Facts label is like the instruction card on a board game — it tells you what's inside, how to use it, and what to watch out for.

### Question 9

The active ingredient is the 'hero' of the medicine — the part that does the job — and it's written right at the top of the label's fact box.

### Question 10

Sometimes a medicine 'graduates' — after the FDA studies it and decides people can use it safely on their own, it moves from needing a note to being on the open shelf.

### Question 11

It's like pouring from a small cup and a big cup into the same bowl — they may hold the same juice, so you could end up with way too much without realizing it.

### Question 12

Vitamins and herbs are more like foods than medicines in the eyes of the law — the FDA doesn't give them the same 'this works to fix a disease' stamp it gives real drugs.

### Question 13

Even 'natural' helpers can mix badly with other medicines, so they need to go on the list too — like writing down every snack, not just the main meals.

### Question 14

OTC medicines are safe when you follow the rules on the box — but break the rules or mix them with other medicines, and they can still cause trouble.

### Question 15

Two medicines can fight the same symptom, but one needs a doctor to steer it because it's harder to use safely on your own.

### Question 16

Some items stay behind the counter like a library's special books — you have to ask the librarian, and sometimes show an ID, before you can borrow them.

### Question 17

People often forget to mention the stuff they bought themselves, but those can still bump into other medicines — so the assistant asks about them on purpose.

### Question 18

If someone says they eat 'a snack sometimes,' you'd ask which snack and how much — the assistant does the same with medicine to get the real details.

### Question 19

Writing down a medicine is like writing a recipe: you need the name, how strong, how much, and how often — not what the box looks like.

### Question 20

Even medicine you only take 'when needed' goes on the list — like noting you keep an umbrella for rainy days even if you don't use it every day.

### Question 21

People tell the truth about their medicine when they feel safe and not judged — like a friend who shares more when you ask kindly.

### Question 22

Two different boxes of cold medicine can hide the same medicine inside — like two different cookie packages that both have chocolate chips, so you'd get way too many.

### Question 23

The medicine list is like the class roster — everyone who shows up gets a name on the list, including the ones you bought yourself.

### Question 24

Even the 'extras' you add to your day — vitamins, fish oil, pain pills — get written down, because they can mix with other things in your body.

### Question 25

Writing the real ingredient name is like naming the fruit ('apple') instead of just the brand of the juice — everyone knows what's actually inside.

### Question 26

If you see a bottle and the person says 'I don't take medicine,' you kindly ask again — sometimes they just didn't think that bottle counted.

### Question 27

Reconciliation is like checking your packing list against what's actually in your suitcase and fixing any mismatches before the trip.

### Question 28

The whole point is safety — making sure a person isn't missing a medicine, taking the same one twice, or taking two that fight each other.

### Question 29

Whenever a patient moves from one place to another in their care — like changing classrooms between periods — the medicine list gets double-checked.

### Question 30

Step one is making the full list of everything the person takes — like gathering every single item on the counter before you start checking.

### Question 31

A BPMH is like a detective's case file — you ask the person, check with family, and look at the pharmacy records to build the truest picture.

### Question 32

Bringing every bottle — even the ones bought at the store — is like bringing every puzzle piece so the whole picture can be seen.

### Question 33

If the list and the orders don't match, the assistant is like the person who raises a hand and says 'these two don't agree' — the doctor is the one who fixes it.

### Question 34

Duplicate therapy is accidentally taking the same medicine twice under two different names — like getting double portions because two dishes secretly had the same filling.

### Question 35

If the patient is taking a medicine that isn't on the doctor's list, that's a missing puzzle piece that needs the doctor's attention.

### Question 36

The truest answer comes from looking at the real bottles and asking the person who takes them — not just guessing or asking someone else.

### Question 37

The assistant is the careful note-taker who gathers and double-checks the list, then hands any problems to the doctor — like a scorekeeper who flags a miscount to the referee.

### Question 38

Verifying is making sure the list is right — like proofreading your homework before turning it in.

### Question 39

After a hospital stay, the medicine list often changes — so the team lines up the old list, the hospital list, and what the patient takes now to spot any differences.

### Question 40

Some medicines and even some herbs all 'thin the blood,' and stacking them up can be risky — the assistant makes sure the doctor sees the whole pile.

### Question 41

The last step is sharing the corrected list — like handing the finished map to the next driver so they don't get lost.

### Question 42

A full medicine list is like a full ingredient list — without it, someone might accidentally mix things that don't go together.

### Question 43

Two medicines with the same secret ingredient can add up to too much — like two glasses of the same strong juice turning into one very full cup.

### Question 44

Writing down what a person is allergic to is like putting a big 'do not touch' sign on the dangerous ingredient.

### Question 45

If someone forgets their list, you don't guess — you ask them to bring the bottles or get the pharmacy's records, like checking the real menu instead of inventing it.

### Question 46

The medicine list is like a grocery list for a busy household — it changes all the time, so you check it every trip.

### Question 47

If a medicine is no longer being taken, you cross it off the list with a note — like updating the roster when someone leaves the team.

### Question 48

OTC medicines can change how other medicines work — like adding an extra ingredient that changes the whole recipe.

### Question 49

Before an operation, doctors need to know everything a person takes — even herbs and store-bought pills — because some can make bleeding or sleep medicines act differently.

### Question 50

The EHR is a shared notebook everyone on the team can read and update — but it only says what someone wrote in it.

### Question 51

New medicine gets written down right away, with all its details — like adding a new ingredient to the recipe card the moment you start using it.

### Question 52

'No known changes' means someone checked the list with the patient and everything still matched — like confirming your packing list before you zip the suitcase.

### Question 53

If the same medicine shows up twice with different names, the assistant points it out so the doctor can fix it — like flagging two identical items on a grocery list.

### Question 54

Before adding a new medicine, the doctor checks the whole list to make sure it won't clash with what's already there.

### Question 55

Sometimes a store-bought stomach tablet can change how another medicine works — and the team only catches that if the stomach tablet is written down.

### Question 56

The assistant asks everyone, every time — because anyone might be taking something from the store shelf that matters.

### Question 57

Some cold medicines can push blood pressure up, so the assistant makes sure the doctor knows the patient is using one.

### Question 58

The assistant writes down what the person really said, then asks more to get it exact — like a careful note-taker who checks their spelling.

### Question 59

When a question mixes a strong medicine with a store-bought one, the assistant says 'let's ask the doctor or pharmacist' and writes it down — not 'sure, go ahead.'

### Question 60

If a dose is smudged or unclear, you ask until it's clear — you never fill in a blank with a guess.

### Question 61

Everything the person takes — and what they're allergic to — goes on the list, like listing every ingredient in a recipe.

### Question 62

If the list is missing something, the team might mix medicines that don't go together — like baking without knowing one ingredient is already in the bowl.

### Question 63

If something the person takes is missing from their list, you ask and add it — like noticing a missing ingredient and fixing the recipe card.

### Question 64

To stop mistakes before they happen, the team checks the list every time things change — like buckling up before every car ride, not after a crash.

### Question 65

Two different boxes can hide the same medicine, so a person might get a double dose without meaning to.

### Question 66

After a hospital stay, the medicine list often changes, so handing it off carefully is like passing the baton in a relay — drop it and someone could get hurt.

### Question 67

The assistant gathers the list and raises any flags; the doctor makes the calls — like the scorekeeper who reports the score but never changes the rules.

### Question 68

Writing down where the info came from is like citing your source in a report — it tells everyone how trustworthy it is and who to double-check with.

### Question 69

Two sleepy-making medicines can stack up into extra sleepiness — the assistant points it out so the doctor can check.

### Question 70

Asking the patient to double-check the list is like letting the person who packed the bag make sure nothing is missing before the trip.

### Question 71

A good, complete list helps the team dodge mistakes — like a full map helping you avoid wrong turns, even if you still watch the road.

### Question 72

Just because a product was easy to order online doesn't mean it can't mix badly with other medicines — so it goes on the list too.

### Question 73

The list gets refreshed right at the start, like sharpening your pencil before you begin drawing.

### Question 74

Medicine prescribed for one person shouldn't be shared — like not wearing someone else's eyeglasses just because you both squint.

### Question 75

A complete medicine list is the team's map — with it, everyone can make safe choices; without it, they're driving blind.
